{{short description|American physicist}}
{{distinguish|Mathieu Koss}}
'''Matthew B. Koss''' (born September 16, 1961, in [[Boston, Massachusetts]]) is a widely published [[Solid-state physics|solid-state physicist]].

==Biography==
Koss received his [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B. degree]] from [[Vassar College]] in 1983 and a Ph.D. in experimental [[condensed matter physics]] from [[Tufts University]] in 1989.

From 1990 to 2000, Koss worked at [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] as Lead Scientist for the Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment (IDGE), a basic [[microgravity]] research project on [[Dendrite (crystal)|dendritic solidification]] that conducted [[Space Shuttle]] flight experiments on [[STS-62]], [[STS-75|-75]] and [[STS-87|-87]]. He also worked as the principal investigator of the Transient Dendritic Solidification Experiment (TDSE),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.org/details/MSFC-0003753 |title=Transient Dendritic Solidification Experiment (TDSE) |publisher=NASA/Marshall Space Flight Center |date=July 7, 2000 |via=[[Wayback Machine]]}}</ref> a flight experiment intended for use on the [[International Space Station]] in 2006.

In June 2003, Koss created controversy via an [[editorial]] published in ''[[The New York Times]]'', in which he wrote that scientists bore partial responsibility for the [[Space Shuttle Columbia disaster|Space Shuttle ''Columbia'' disaster]]. He argued that most microgravity scientific experiments did not require crewed space missions, but were used to promote the space program.<ref name="June2003NYT">{{cite news |first=Matthew B. |last=Koss |title=How Science Brought Down the Shuttle |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/06/29/opinion/how-science-brought-down-the-shuttle.html |work=The New York Times |page=13 |date=June 29, 2003 |accessdate=April 10, 2022 |via=nytimes.com}}</ref> The article drew widespread attention, and Koss later appeared at a congressional hearing before the [[House Science Committee]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/99512996/panel-says-nasa-should-abandon-shuttle-p/ |title=Panel says NASA should abandon shuttle program |first=Gwyneth K. |last=Shaw |agency=[[Knight Ridder]] |newspaper=[[The Bradenton Herald]] |location=[[Bradenton, Florida]] |page=7 |date=October 17, 2003 |accessdate=April 10, 2022 |via=newspapers.com}}</ref>

In 2000, Koss started working at [[College of the Holy Cross]] in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]], where he continued his isothermal dendritic growth research. As of April 2008, Koss was an associate professor of physics at Holy Cross.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/99513468/a-thin-envelope-a-full-life/ |title=A thin envelope, a full life |first=Matthew B. |last=Koss |newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] |page=15 |date=April 28, 2008 |accessdate=April 10, 2022 |via=newspapers.com}}</ref> He remains listed as a professor in the Holy Cross physics department {{as of|2022|4|lc=yes}}.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.holycross.edu/academics/programs/physics/faculty/matthew-koss |title=Matthew Koss |website=holycross.edu |accessdate=April 10, 2022}}</ref>

In 2005, Koss began research on the physics of [[baseball]]. He collected data on a baseball in flight to create his own [[Reynolds number]] vs. [[drag coefficient]] plot, to compare against other models.  He also created a hybrid model of the flight path that a baseball will take, given all of the initial conditions. He also worked to add other factors that would affect the flight, such as the spin decay rate of a baseball in flight.
